did_you_know.text: Egypt and Canaan were different regions of the ancient Near East, with Egypt to the south and Canaan to its northeast. The verse warns Israel not to adopt automatically the customs of either the society they left or the one they were entering.

In Jewish interpretation, “judgments” and “statutes” came to represent two kinds of commandments: rules whose reasons are easier to understand and rules whose reasons are not always clear. The verse emphasizes that both understanding and obedience matter.

The Sages interpreted “you shall live by them” to mean that the commandments are meant to sustain life, not cause a person to die because of them. This became an important basis for the principle of saving a life.

“Born in the house” and “born outside” do not refer to where someone lived; they describe a sister who shares the same father or the same mother. In other words, the verse includes both full and half-sisters.

“Your son’s daughter” and “your daughter’s daughter” are the biblical terms for a granddaughter, so the prohibition also includes the generation after one’s children. The verse uses precise family terms to avoid misunderstanding.

Genesis tells that Jacob was married to Leah and Rachel, who were sisters; Leviticus 18, however, forbids marrying a woman and her sister during their lifetimes. The contrast shows that the Torah presents a rule different from the earlier story.

Molech is a name associated in the Bible with the offering of children, although scholars debate the exact details of the ritual. Linking this prohibition with profaning God’s name emphasizes the seriousness of the act.

The word “abomination” is a strong biblical term for an act considered deeply wrong or detestable. It appears in several different contexts in the Bible, so its meaning must be understood from each passage’s context.

The phrase “the land vomited out its inhabitants” is personification: the land is described as if it could vomit people out. This image presents a society’s actions as something that can cause it to lose its place in the land.

“The stranger who lives among you” refers to a resident foreigner, not merely a passing visitor. Including the resident stranger alongside the citizen shows that the chapter’s moral expectations apply to everyone living in the land.
